title: Only about half of 18-month-olds know the baby in the mirror is them

cover.alt: Close-up photograph of a chimpanzee’s face, looking slightly to one side.

body: In 1970 Gordon Gallup Jr. anaesthetised chimpanzees, dabbed odourless red dye on an eyebrow ridge and the opposite ear, then gave them a mirror. The chimps touched the marks on their own faces, showing they knew the reflection was their own body. This ‘mark test’ has since been passed by bonobos, orangutans, bottlenose dolphins and at least one Asian elephant, while dogs and most monkeys treat the reflection as another animal or ignore it. Human children get there gradually: in a 1974 study about half recognised themselves at 18 months, and more a few months later. Critics such as Frans de Waal warn that self-awareness is not a yes-or-no switch, and that the test favours animals that rely on sight.

slides.question: Out of 20 children aged 20 to 24 months, how many recognise themselves in the mirror?
slides.explanation: About 65% by 20 to 24 months, in the rouge test, where a spot of make-up is put on the child’s face before the mirror is shown.

steps.label: An odourless mark is placed out of its sight
It touches the mark on its own body: pass

slides.heading: Who passes
items: One of three Asian elephants tested in 2006
Not dogs or most monkeys: they see a stranger or lose interest

slides.alt: Close-up portrait of a Eurasian magpie, a black-and-white bird with glossy blue-green wing feathers.
slides.caption: In 2008 Eurasian magpies were reported as the first non-mammals to pass. A 2020 replication with more birds failed to confirm the result.

slides.heading: The sniff test
slides.text: Dogs live by smell, so a visual test may be unfair to them. In 2017 Alexandra Horowitz gave dogs samples of their own urine, some with an added scent ‘mark’. The dogs spent longer investigating their own altered odour, the scent-world equivalent of touching a mark seen in a mirror.

slides.question: Why do some scientists doubt that cleaner wrasse fish really passed the test in 2019?
options: The mark looked like a parasite
slides.explanation: Gordon Gallup, who devised the mark test in 1970, argued the fish may simply have reacted to what looked like a parasite, which cleaner fish remove for a living. The study’s authors disagree.
